newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens say Russian jets intercept official plane.
newsitem.headline: Chechens say Russian jets intercept official plane.

text.p: Separatist officials in Chechnya alleged that Russian jets forced an airliner carrying the region's vice-president to abort a flight abroad on Tuesday.

Russian officials were unavailable for comment on the incident, which posed the first major test of a peace treaty with Chechnya signed just a week ago in Moscow. The Chechen government will meet in emergency session early on Wednesday.
"This is a provocation by the Russians aimed at wrecking the peace treaty," First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov told Reuters in the Chechen capital, Grozny.
"It is a gross violation by the Russians," said Vice-President Vakha Arsanov, whose flight was intercepted.
He was later reported to have demanded that Russian officials quit Chechnya, although other Chechen leaders said this was not the official position of the Grozny government.

Arsanov told Reuters that Russian officials had given him permission to fly direct to the Netherlands across Russian air space for a conference in The Hague at the invitation of the Dutch foreign ministry.
But scarcely had he taken off from Grozny when Russian radio operators ordered the pilot to land at the south Russian town of Mineralniye Vody, 250 km (150 miles) northwest of the city.
Arsanov refused and turned back. Two Russian fighters accompanied the plane back to the Chechen frontier, he said.

Interfax news agency quoted Arsanov as saying he would give Russian government officials in Chechnya, including President Boris Yeltsin's personal representative, until noon (0800 GMT) on Wednesday to leave the region.
Udugov told Reuters he had spoken to Kremlin Security Council secretary Ivan Rybkin, the main Russian peace negotiator, and lodged an official protest over the incident.
He gave no details of Rybkin's response.
Russian officials were not available for comment. RIA news agency quoted a Defence Ministry duty officer as saying he could neither confirm nor deny the Chechen allegations.
The Chechen government was to meet at 9 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Wednesday to discuss the events, Udugov said.

Chechnya would urge Yeltsin to punish those involved. The Chechens -- and Russian liberals -- have regularly complained that there is a "party of war" in Moscow which has profited from the conflict in the region and wants to prolong it.
Twenty-one months of fighting that followed Yeltsin's decision to sent in the army to crush the separatists in December 1994 left tens of thousands dead.
Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov and Yeltsin finally signed what is intended to be a lasting peace treaty in Moscow on May 12. Both pledged it would end four centuries of conflict.

While Yeltsin went a long way to recognising the Chechens' autonomy and Russia agreed to start helping to rebuild the region's shattered economy, the treaty left open the vexed issue of whether Chechnya will ever be a sovereign state.
This is Maskhadov's aim, although he has promised never to resort to force and has ordered Chechnya's irregular guerrilla groups to disband, thus limiting his armed forces.
Yeltsin refuses to countenance full independence. Some Russian nationalists feel he has already gone too far.
